title: AI Tutors vs. Tenacious Myths: Evidence from Personalised Dialogue Interventions in Education
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether personalized AI dialogue can more effectively reduce stubborn misconceptions in psychology and education than traditional static corrective materials. The authors focus on common myths such as learning styles and the “10% of the brain” belief, arguing that these misconceptions are resistant to standard refutation because they are tied to intuitive thinking and confirmation bias. The study asks whether an AI tutor that engages participants in tailored back-and-forth conversation can produce stronger and more lasting belief change than either a textbook-style refutation passage or a neutral AI conversation.

In a preregistered experiment, 375 adults recruited via Prolific were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) a personalized three-round AI dialogue using Claude 3.5 Sonnet that targeted each participant’s strongest misconception, (2) a textbook-reading condition with a static refutation passage on the same misconception, or (3) a neutral AI dialogue control on unrelated topics. Participants first rated belief in 16 psychology misconceptions, then received an intervention tailored to their highest-rated misconception. Outcomes were measured immediately after the intervention, again after 10 days, and again after 2 months using repeated belief ratings and post-intervention self-reports of engagement and confidence.

The study was conducted online using Qualtrics and Prolific with English-fluent adults who had to endorse at least one misconception above a threshold to be eligible. The intervention context was not a formal school classroom; rather, it was an online experimental setting involving members of the general adult population. No teachers were involved in delivery. The AI conditions used live API-based conversational interaction, while the textbook condition used matched-length static reading passages.

The main finding is that personalized AI dialogue produced the largest immediate reduction in belief in the targeted misconception, outperforming both textbook reading and neutral AI dialogue. This advantage persisted at the 10-day follow-up but was no longer statistically distinguishable from textbook reading at 2 months, although both corrective conditions remained better than the neutral control. Both AI conditions also produced higher self-reported engagement and confidence than textbook reading. However, none of the interventions reduced non-targeted misconceptions, suggesting that the benefits were specific to the addressed belief rather than generalized critical thinking gains. The authors conclude that AI tutoring is promising for accelerating initial misconception correction, but that brief one-off interactions likely need reinforcement to sustain long-term advantages.

identified_tools.name: Claude
identified_tools.description: Anthropic's large language model family used as a conversational AI system for interactive dialogue.
identified_tools.use_case: Claude was used via API in Qualtrics to deliver a three-round personalized misconception-refutation dialogue targeting each participant's strongest psychology misconception, and also to power a neutral AI dialogue control on unrelated topics.

findings.finding_summary: In a preregistered randomized experiment, the personalized Claude-based misconception dialogue produced significantly lower immediate post-intervention belief in participants' strongest misconception than both neutral AI dialogue and textbook reading, controlling for pre-intervention belief. Post-intervention means were Misconception AI M=50.68 (SD=31.51), Neutral AI M=85.88 (SD=16.99), and Textbook Reading M=61.47 (SD=32.83); the Misconception AI vs Neutral AI mean difference was 36.55 (SE=3.43), 95% CI [29.80, 43.30], t(371)=10.65, p<.001, and Misconception AI vs Textbook difference was 9.77 (SE=3.43), 95% CI [3.02, 16.52], t(371)=2.85, p=.013.
findings.measure: Belief rating in highest-rated misconception on a 0-100 scale, immediately post-intervention

findings.finding_summary: For participants with complete longitudinal data, the personalized Claude-based misconception dialogue maintained lower belief ratings than both comparison conditions at 10 days. At 10 days, Misconception AI was lower than Neutral AI by 29.1 points, 95% CI [19.52, 38.70], t(307)=-7.16, p<.001, and lower than Textbook Reading by 12.2 points, 95% CI [3.04, 21.30], t(307)=-3.14, p=.005.
findings.measure: Belief rating in highest-rated misconception at 10-day follow-up

findings.finding_summary: By 2 months, the personalized Claude-based misconception dialogue remained superior to Neutral AI but was no longer statistically different from Textbook Reading. Misconception AI differed from Neutral AI by 19.95 points, 95% CI [10.28, 29.60], t(307)=-4.86, p<.001, while the Misconception AI vs Textbook Reading contrast was -8.11 points, 95% CI [-17.3, 1.12], t(307)=-2.07, p≈.10.
findings.measure: Belief rating in highest-rated misconception at 2-month follow-up

findings.finding_summary: The Claude-based misconception dialogue did not produce broader reductions in non-targeted misconceptions relative to textbook or neutral AI conditions. Repeated-measures ANCOVA found no significant main effect of Intervention Type, F(2, 307)=1.42, p=.24, no main effect of Time, F(2, 614)=2.24, p=.108, and no Condition × Time interaction, F(4, 614)=1.52, p=.20.
findings.measure: Mean belief ratings for non-targeted misconceptions across post, 10-day, and 2-month assessments

findings.finding_summary: Participants in both Claude-based AI dialogue conditions reported higher engagement than textbook reading. Misconception AI engagement was M=84.86 (SD=17.30) versus Textbook Reading M=75.36 (SD=21.19), mean difference=9.50, 95% CI [3.72, 15.28], p<.001; Neutral AI engagement was M=81.50 (SD=19.57) and also exceeded Textbook Reading by 6.14, 95% CI [0.36, 11.92], p=.034.

Participants in both Claude-based AI dialogue conditions reported higher confidence than textbook reading, though the personalized misconception dialogue was not significantly different from neutral AI dialogue. Misconception AI confidence was M=76.29 (SD=19.19) versus Textbook Reading M=63.29 (SD=21.22), mean difference=13.00, 95% CI [7.24, 18.76], p<.001; Neutral AI confidence was M=80.16 (SD=17.45), exceeding Textbook Reading by 16.87, 95% CI [11.11, 22.63], p<.001.
findings.measure: Self-reported confidence in explaining the discussed topics (0-100)

quality_tier_rationale: This is a preregistered randomized experiment with a reasonably large sample (N=375) and follow-up measurement, which strengthens causal inference. However, it is a preprint not yet peer reviewed, and some reporting lacks standardized effect sizes, so it falls short of blue.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports clear positive immediate and short-term effects on targeted misconception belief reduction, with sizeable mean differences, but the advantage over textbook reading attenuates by 2 months and no generalized transfer was found. Because standardized effect sizes are not reported and durability is mixed, the impact is best rated as green rather than blue.
